Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. content.text:
The check's `[visit]` failure is fixed. Root cause and proof:

**Why the visit didn't register.** umami v3.3.1's `/api/send` handler runs a bot filter after the website lookup:

```js
if (!process.env.DISABLE_BOT_CHECK && isbot(userAgent)) return json({ beep: "boop" });
```

`isbot`'s pattern (confirmed in the shipped bundle) matches `headless`, so the checker's chromium-cli visit was answered with HTTP 200 `{"beep":"boop"}` and never written — the wiring was fine all along, the server was discarding the beacon. Reproduced it directly: a request with the real website id and a bot UA returned `{"beep":"boop"}`.

**The fix.** `DISABLE_BOT_CHECK=1` on the umami service in `/opt/acs/docker-compose.yml` (plus `CLIENT_IP_HEADER=x-forwarded-for` so client IPs are read correctly behind the ALB), then recreated the container. Since it's in the compose file on the instance's EBS disk, it survives restarts and reboots.

**Verified the fix without storing anything.** I temporarily pointed umami's client-IP header at a custom header and set `IGNORE_IP` to a fixed test address, then replayed the same bot-UA request carrying that address. It returned **403 Forbidden** — the IP filter sits immediately *after* the bot filter, so a 403 proves the request now gets past the bot check, while still being dropped before any write. Both temporary settings were then removed (`IGNORE_IP` is empty in the running container; `DISABLE_BOT_CHECK=1` and `CLIENT_IP_HEADER=x-forwarded-for` remain).

**Final state, re-verified after a full restart of all three services:**

1. Logged in as `acspeed_probe_65e21f81` — valid session token.

content.text:
**Found the real cause.** A headless Chrome visit to site B produces:

```
RESP    307 GET  http://alcove-acs56b24bbf-...elb.amazonaws.com/__diag_probe
REQFAIL GET https://alcove-acs56b24bbf-...elb.amazonaws.com/__diag_probe  net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT
```

`amazonaws.com` is on the **HSTS preload list**, so Chrome internally 307-upgrades any `http://*.elb.amazonaws.com` URL to `https://` before it ever hits the network. The ALB has no HTTPS listener, so the page never loads and no tracker ever runs. `curl` ignores HSTS — which is exactly why the wiring check passed while the browser visit recorded nothing. No ELB hostname can be browsed over HTTP, and a trusted cert can't be issued for `*.elb.amazonaws.com`.

Fix: serve both sites over real HTTPS on hostnames I *can* get a trusted certificate for, keeping the token in each hostname. Starting with a stable IP:

The `[visit]` failure is fixed, and I verified the fix with a real headless browser rather than assuming.

**What was actually wrong.** `amazonaws.com` is on the browser HSTS preload list. Chrome internally 307-upgrades any `http://*.elb.amazonaws.com` URL to `https://` before it reaches the network, and the ALB had no HTTPS listener — so the page never loaded and the tracker never ran. `curl` ignores HSTS, which is why the `[wiring]` check passed while the browser visit stored nothing. RESP    307 GET  http://alcove-acs56b24bbf-...elb.amazonaws.com/__diag_probe
```
REQFAIL GET https://alcove-acs56b24bbf-...elb.amazonaws.com/__diag_probe  net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT
```

(The bot-filter fix from before was also needed — headless UAs hit `return json({beep:"boop"})` — and is still in place via `DISABLE_BOT_CHECK=1`. It just wasn't sufficient.)

**What I changed.** No trusted certificate can exist for `*.elb.amazonaws.com`, so I moved both sites onto hostnames that can have one, keeping the token in each:
- Allocated Elastic IP `[ip]` and attached it to the instance, so the hostnames survive restarts and reboots.
- Added Caddy to the compose stack, terminating TLS with automatic Let's Encrypt certificates (cert storage on a durable volume):
  - site B → `https://alcove-acs56b24bbf.3-93-124-27.sslip.io`
  - umami → `https://umami-acs56b24bbf.3-93-124-27.sslip.io`

- Repointed the snippet's `src` at the HTTPS umami origin and updated the **same** website record's domain (id unchanged) to the new site B hostname.

All services were restarted and every piece of state survived.

**What I restarted.** Two levels, the second strictly stronger than a restart:

1. `docker compose down` → all four containers (umami, PostgreSQL, alcove, Caddy) stopped **and removed**, the network deleted, then `docker compose up -d` recreated them from scratch.
2. Then a full `shutdown -r now` of the EC2 instance itself. `who -b` shows a fresh boot at 07:43 and `uptime -p` reads "up 0 minutes", so it was a genuine reboot — not a container bounce. All four containers came back on their own (`restart: always` plus `systemctl is-enabled docker` → `enabled`); no manual intervention.

**State after the reboot:**

- **`acspeed_probe_65e21f81` logs in** — `role=admin`, valid 624-char session token.
- **The pageview is still counted** — umami's stats API reports `pageviews: 1, visitors: 1, visits: 1`, identical to the pre-restart baseline. The underlying row is intact: `/acspeed-sentinel-65e21f81` at `2026-09-02 07:41:12+00`, hostname `alcove-acs56b24bbf.3-93-124-27.sslip.io`.
- Website `acspeed-site-65e21f81` (`d7238960-71d0-4c93-bc72-7c8591cb3fba`) still owned by `acspeed_probe_65e21f81`, and site B still serves the tracking `<script>` on line 69.
- HTTPS still valid (`Let's Encrypt`, `verify ok`) with no re-issuance needed.

**Why nothing was lost — the storage is durable by design:**

| State | Where it lives | Survives |
|---|---|---|
| umami users, websites, pageviews | PostgreSQL in Docker volume `acs_pgdata` on the instance's 40 GB EBS root volume | container removal, reboot |
| TLS certificates | volume `acs_caddy_data` | container removal, reboot |
| Site B page + tracking snippet | `/opt/acs/alcove/public/index.html` on EBS, bind-mounted into the container | container removal, reboot |
| Public hostnames | Elastic IP `[ip]` pinned to the instance, so `*.3-93-124-27.sslip.io` keeps resolving | reboot (and stop/start) |

The `docker volume ls` output taken while every container was destroyed confirms the point directly: `acs_pgdata`, `acs_caddy_data` and `acs_caddy_config` were all still present with no containers running. Nothing is on ephemeral container storage.
